title: The big lookout
hookLine: year one ends: look back down the hill, then up

lines: A FLAT ROCK, A RAIL, A BENCH.
THE TRAIL BELOW, THE RANGES BEYOND.
cards: At the top of the hill there's a lookout. A flat rock, a rail, maybe a bench someone carved their initials into. This is day three hundred thirty-one of the climb.
Maybe some days you ran. Maybe some you crawled. Maybe on a few you sat down on the path and didn't move, and that counted too.
Below you, the whole trail, switchbacks and all, back down to the spot where you took one breath with a bell. Above and beyond, the ranges. For one day, you get to stand in the middle and see both.

teach.b: Look down at the camps. The first words, starting with breathe. The stories: a shipwreck, a butterfly, a carob tree.
The practices: the breath, the evening review, the sunset. The text: Rumi's reed, with Marcus beside him. Then this last camp, the depths, the longest of all.

teach.h: SEVEN HOMES, THE PORCH, THE LAB.
teach.b: You went as a guest into seven homes. Hinduism: dharma, and you are that. Buddhism: wake up, and may all beings be well.
Judaism: hear, and repair. Christianity: love your neighbor, and grace. The Catholic tradition: the rosary and the works of mercy.
Islam: one God, and hearts that find rest in remembrance. Sikhism: the name, honest work, and the free kitchen. Then home to the Stoic porch: character, the four virtues, the citadel.
Then the lab: resonance breathing, sixty-six days, take it for a walk somewhere green, a mirror, not a forecast, and Hume's gap between is and ought. Then the doors: every door stays open.
Now a line from a tradition that loved hills.

teach.h: I WILL LIFT UP MINE EYES.
teach.b: A psalm, in the King James words: "I will lift up mine eyes unto the hills, from whence cometh my help." The next verse answers: the help comes from God, the maker of heaven and earth.
The King James Bible heads this psalm a song of degrees, and tradition links those songs with pilgrims going up to Jerusalem.

teach.h: A THOUSAND LI, A SINGLE STEP.
teach.b: And one from the Tao Te Ching, in James Legge's translation: "The journey of a thousand li commenced with a single step."
You took that step on day one. Every step since was also a single step. That's all a year is.
Tomorrow, the porch: year two opens with a little handbook meant to be kept at hand.

how: Many people mark the end of a long stretch of practice by going somewhere high or open, looking back over what they did, and naming what comes next.

o: a mountain guide in the old pilgrim songs
a hymn writer who set the psalms to music
the poet whose reed flute opened the text camp

games.q: year one, from the top — tap the pairs.

a year only counts if you never missed a day

games.q: you're at the lookout at the end of year one. where do you look?
o: only back, at what you missed.
down at the trail, then up at the ranges.
only ahead, at what's still left.
games.why: the lookout is for both: look how far you came, then look up. tomorrow, year two begins.

practice: Stand somewhere high if you can, a hill, a balcony, the top of the stairs, or a window, and look down: let the year pass below you, a face, a story, a hard week, a good one.
Then take one breath, the same as day one, and look up at the sky, between the trail below and the open sky.

wordCard.voice: Rumi, whose reed appears at the big lookout: look back down the whole trail, then up at the ranges. The year's last word.

carryVoice: Your line: look how far. You've earned the rest. Year one, done.
